analysis.one_liner: Requires rent-to-own stores to disclose the total cost to own and gives customers basic payment and reinstatement rights.
analysis.headline: The rent-to-own disclosure bill drew 40 bipartisan cosponsors but never received a hearing or vote, dying in a House subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set the first federal consumer rules for rent-to-own stores: disclose the total cost to own before signing, post the cash price and number of payments on merchandise and in ads, let customers reinstate after missed payments, and ban practices like wage assignments and confessions of judgment. It also would have preempted state laws that require stores to reveal an annual percentage rate or treat the deals as credit. Referred to a House Financial Services subcommittee in May 2005, it never got a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Lower-income households that rent furniture, appliances, and electronics to own — about 2.3 million households a year by the bill's own findings — would get clear upfront disclosure of what ownership actually costs, the right to reinstate after falling behind, and protection from wage assignments and stacked late fees. Rent-to-own merchants would also gain: a single federal framework treating their contracts as leases rather than credit, with state APR-disclosure laws preempted.

how_it_helps.text: Before signing, merchants would have to disclose the total cost to acquire ownership, the cash price, and the number of payments — in the contract, on tags next to the merchandise, and in any advertisement that quotes a payment.

Customers who miss a payment or return the item would get set windows to reinstate the agreement without losing rights already accrued — at least 60 days, extended to 120 days for anyone who has paid half the total cost.

Agreements could no longer contain confessions of judgment, wage assignments, or waivers of legal claims; loss-and-damage charges would be capped at the lowest of fair market value, the early-purchase price, or repair cost, and only one late fee could be charged per missed payment.
A merchant could not charge any fee beyond the disclosed total as a condition of finally taking ownership of the item.
The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would gain enforcement power, with civil liability for violations and criminal penalties for willful, knowing violations.

analysis.who_pays: Rent-to-own merchants would bear compliance costs, civil liability, and new limits on fees. Consumers in states with stronger laws would also give something up: the bill overrides state rules that require an annual percentage rate disclosure or classify these contracts as credit, so shoppers in those states could lose the one number that makes rent-to-own costs comparable to other financing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Rent-to-own merchants, plus shoppers in stricter states

drawbacks.text: The bill would supersede any state law that requires disclosure of a percentage rate — an annual percentage rate or equivalent — or that treats rent-to-own deals as credit sales. Since rent-to-own totals often run to multiples of the cash price, removing the APR comparison would make it harder for shoppers to see how expensive the deal is next to a loan or layaway.

The bill sets no ceiling on what stores can charge. A store could still collect several times the cash price for a television, as long as it discloses the total — the remedy for overpricing is a number on a page, not a limit.

The Federal Reserve could exempt independent small businesses from the requirement to return the same or a comparable item during extended reinstatement, and could loosen other rules by regulation, so the protections in practice would depend on how regulators wrote them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For shoppers in states with no rent-to-own rules, the disclosure and reinstatement rights would be a real gain, and the ban on wage assignments and confession-of-judgment clauses would close genuine abuses. But the same bill would shield the industry's core pricing structure: it bars states from requiring an annual percentage rate and locks in the lease classification that keeps these transactions outside credit law. The bill helps and hobbles the same shoppers, and how much either side weighs depends entirely on the state a customer lives in.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Financial Services subcommittee on financial institutions for the rest of the two-year Congress and never received a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Walter Jones introduced the bill on April 14, 2005, with five original cosponsors from both parties, including Reps. Kanjorski (D-PA) and Hensarling (R-TX).
The House referred it to the Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and on May 19, 2005 the committee sent it to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit.

No hearing, markup, or vote ever followed. Over 40 members cosponsored the bill — 30 Republicans and 10 Democrats — but it never left the subcommittee, and it died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rent-to-own merchants came out ahead: with no law, they kept operating under whatever state rules applied, kept the lease classification wherever states allowed it, and owed nothing new. Customers in states without their own protections were left with no federal floor.

for.name: Walter B. Jones Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 14, 2005 and recruited bipartisan original cosponsors.

for.name: Paul Kanjorski
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-PA), senior member of the Financial Services panel handling the bill
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor the day the bill was introduced.

for.name: Rent-to-own industry trade association
for.what_they_did: Backed this long-running federal bill, which would give the industry a uniform national framework treating its contracts as leases rather than credit.

against.name: Michael Oxley
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill up at the full-committee level; it was routed to a subcommittee and stayed there.

against.name: Richard Baker
against.role: Chair, Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the eighteen months it sat in his subcommittee.

against.name: Consumer advocacy groups (e.g., Consumer Federation of America, Consumers Union)
against.what_they_did: Opposed comparable federal rent-to-own bills because the preemption clause would erase stronger state laws requiring an annual percentage rate disclosure.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 40 cosponsors split 30 Republicans and 10 Democrats — but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of any opposition never showed.

industries.industry: Rent-to-own chains (furniture, appliance, and electronics rental)
industries.note: The bill would have codified the industry's defining feature — these contracts are leases, not credit — and barred states from requiring an annual percentage rate or reclassifying the deals as credit sales, while adding disclosure, reinstatement, and fee rules. That trade is why the same bill helps customers see the total cost and helps the industry keep the effective rate out of view.
